pos: n. (a niggardly man; one whose instruments are evil, set opposite the liberal)
etymology: Old English ceorl, a common freeman, then by long descent a rude and grasping man. The Hebrew kilay in Isaiah 32 means the crafty, the miserly, the man who deals by fraud.
biblical_def: Isaiah 32 describes the kingdom of the righteous King, and one mark of it is that words go back to meaning what they mean: “The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful” (Isa 32:5). Two lies are broken in one verse. Under the old order the vile man was flattered as generous and the churl was praised as bountiful, because whoever holds the purse also holds the vocabulary. The prophet then shows the churl at work: “The instruments also of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right” (Isa 32:7). He is not merely tight-fisted. He has instruments — means, contrivances, a method — and the method is lying words used against a poor man whose case is honest. Set against him stands one sentence of quiet greatness: “But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand” (Isa 32:8). Both men devise. The difference is what they devise and what they stand on at the last. Proverbs adds the promise that governs a bountiful hand: “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself” (Pro 11:25). The churl keeps and shrinks; the liberal pours and stands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a churl as a rustic or countryman, then a rude, surly, ill-bred man, and particularly a niggard or miser — one of a close and grasping disposition.
webster_full: CHURL, n. [Sax. ceorl, a man, a freeman of the lowest rank.] A rustic; a countryman or labourer.
2. A rude, surly, ill-bred man.
3. A miser; a niggard; a man of a close and grasping disposition.
The churl said to be bountiful. Isa. xxxii.
scriptures: Isa 32:5
The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful.
Isa 32:7
The instruments also of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right.
Isa 32:8
But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand.
The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
corruption_summary: The churl's oldest trick is not hoarding but renaming, and Isaiah 32:5 promises a kingdom in which the flattering name is taken away from him.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse names a corruption of language before it names a corruption of money. A vile man was called liberal; a churl was said to be bountiful. The lie was not told by the churl alone but by the men around him who needed his favour, and it worked because generosity is measured by reputation rather than by what actually reaches the poor. Every age repeats it. A man whose gains are wrung out of the needy endows a wing that carries his name and is thanked publicly for his bounty; the announcement is the gift, and the poor whose case was crushed with lying words are no better fed. Isaiah's promise is that the righteous King restores the plain meaning of words, and that restoration is itself a mercy to the poor, because a man who can no longer buy the name of generous must either become generous or be known.

There is a churlishness that never touches money at all, and Scripture is as severe with it. The churl of Isaiah 32:7 destroys the poor with lying words — his instrument is speech, and his victim is a man whose case is right. That is the churl in the assembly, in the court, in the eldership: the one who cannot be generous with a brother's reputation, who devises a construction of his neighbour's words that no honest hearing would allow. Against him the eighth verse sets the only stability there is. The liberal man stands — not because giving purchases anything, for grace is not bought, but because a bountiful hand is the fruit of a heart that has received freely and therefore has nothing to protect. Nabal, whose very name means folly, is the churl of the histories, and his end is the commentary on this proverb.
roots_summary: Hebrew kilay (H3596), the crafty, churlish, miserly man; contrasted with nadiyb (H5081), the noble, willing, liberal man; both in Isaiah 32.
roots_lines: Hebrew kilay (H3596) — a churl, a knave; the miser whose dealings are fraud; Isaiah 32:5, Isaiah 32:7.
Hebrew nadiyb (H5081) — noble, willing, liberal; the opposite man of the same passage, whose devices are liberal things; Isaiah 32:8.
Hebrew ebyown (H34) — the needy, the man in want who here speaks right and is answered with lying words; Isaiah 32:7.
Hebrew nabal (H5036) — foolish, vile; the root behind the name of the churl of Carmel who railed on David's young men; 1 Samuel 25:25.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the grasping temper the New Testament names as idolatry; Colossians 3:5.
usage: “Nor the churl said to be bountiful” — the flattering name taken away in the King's kingdom.
“The instruments also of the churl are evil” — his weapon is lying words against an honest case.
“By liberal things shall he stand” — the open hand is the standing one.

pos: n. (one born out of lawful marriage; in Hebrews, a son left without chastening)
etymology: Old French bastard, a child born out of wedlock. The Hebrew mamzer is a narrower word, used of the offspring of forbidden unions; the Greek nothos in Hebrews 12 means an unacknowledged son, one the father does not own.
biblical_def: The law shuts a door: “A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to his tenth generation shall he not enter into the congregation of the LORD” (Deu 23:2). The next verse shuts it on Ammon and Moab in the same words (Deu 23:3), which is how the reader learns that the exclusion is covenantal rather than personal spite — it is Israel's assembly being guarded from the fruit of unions God had forbidden. Zechariah turns the word against Philistia: “And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines” (Zec 9:6). Then Hebrews takes the word into the household of grace and makes it a comfort. “But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons” (Heb 12:8). The mark of true sonship is not an easy life but a Father's hand of correction; the man God never disciplines is the man God has not owned. Ruth the Moabitess entering the line of David, and Rahab before her, show what the gospel does with the law's closed door: it does not lower the standard, it brings the outsider in by grace and writes the name into the genealogy of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bastard as a natural child, one begotten and born out of lawful wedlock; and adjectivally, spurious, counterfeit, adulterate, not genuine.
webster_full: BASTARD, n. A natural child; a child begotten and born out of wedlock; an illegitimate or spurious child.
2. In Scripture, one born of an unlawful union.
BASTARD, a. Begotten out of wedlock; illegitimate; spurious; not genuine; false; supposititious; adulterate.
If ye be without chastisement, then are ye bastards, and not sons. Heb. xii.
scriptures: Deu 23:2
A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to his tenth generation shall he not enter into the congregation of the LORD.
Deu 23:3
An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation shall they not enter into the congregation of the LORD for ever:
Heb 12:8
But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.
Zec 9:6
And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 12:8 makes an unchastened life the evidence of no sonship, which is the reverse of the assumption that a smooth providence proves God's favour.
corruption_paragraphs: The Deuteronomy statute is read today as though it punished a child for his parents' sin, and the reading misses what the law is guarding. The congregation of the LORD is not a nation's population but its worshipping assembly, and the door is closed against the visible fruit of unions the law had already named as abominations — the point being that Israel's worship was not to be reorganised around the consequences of Israel's sin. That the same paragraph shuts out Ammon and Moab as peoples, then opens in the third generation to Edom and Egypt, shows the statute working by covenant category and not by personal worth. And Scripture itself supplies the gospel answer within the canon: Ruth the Moabitess is brought in, married, and set in the line of the King, so that the law's closed door and the Redeemer's open one stand in the same Bible without embarrassment.

The corruption that costs Christians most is at Hebrews 12:8, and it runs the argument backwards. Ease is taken for approval and correction for abandonment, so that a man under a hard providence concludes God has cast him off, while a man under no correction at all assumes he is doing well. The apostle says the opposite in one sentence: chastening is the proof of sonship, and its absence is the mark of a son the Father has not acknowledged. That is a severe comfort and it is meant to be. It does not mean every affliction is a rebuke for a particular sin — Job's friends built a whole false theology on that — but it does mean the Father who has adopted a man will not leave him unformed. The right response to the rod is neither despising it nor fainting under it, but the son's response: to be exercised by it, and to yield the peaceable fruit of righteousness.
roots_summary: Hebrew mamzer (H4464), one born of a forbidden union; Greek nothos (G3541), an unacknowledged or illegitimate son; set against huios (G5207), the owned and chastened son.
roots_lines: Hebrew mamzer (H4464) — a bastard, the offspring of a union the law forbade; Deuteronomy 23:2, Zechariah 9:6.
Hebrew qahal (H6951) — the assembly or congregation of the LORD, the worshipping body the statute guards; Deuteronomy 23:2.
Greek nothos (G3541) — illegitimate, a son not owned by the father; Hebrews 12:8, and nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek paideia (G3809) — chastening, the training a father gives a son; Hebrews 12:5-11.
Greek huiothesia (G5206) — adoption, the placing of a son, which is what the bastard by nature receives by grace; Romans 8:15, Ephesians 1:5.
usage: “A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD” — the assembly guarded by covenant law.
“Then are ye bastards, and not sons” — the unchastened life as evidence, not the chastened one.
Ruth the Moabitess in the line of David — what sovereign grace does with a closed door.

pos: n. (an unbeliever; one who has no part with him that believeth)
etymology: Latin infidelis, unfaithful, from in-, not, and fidelis, faithful. The Greek apistos is the plain negative of pistos, believing — the man without faith.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and both places are startling. Paul asks the Corinthians a chain of questions with only one answer: “And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” (2Co 6:15). The infidel there is not a man of another religion in the modern sense but simply the unbeliever, and the apostle's point is that the believer and the unbeliever have no shared foundation on which to be unequally yoked. The second use is the one that stops a professing man in his tracks: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8). Paul does not say such a man is like an infidel; he says he is worse, because the unbeliever who feeds his family at least keeps the natural duty that even a fallen conscience acknowledges, while the professor who neglects his has denied by his hands what he confesses with his mouth. Titus states the principle flatly: “They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him” (Tit 1:16). Faith that provides nothing has confessed nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an infidel as one who disbelieves the inspiration of the Scriptures and the divine origin of Christianity; a disbeliever, distinguished from the heathen who has never had the gospel.
webster_full: INFIDEL, a. [L. infidelis; in and fidelis, faithful.] Unbelieving; disbelieving the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine institution of Christianity.
INFIDEL, n. One who disbelieves the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the divine origin of Christianity.
The word is not applied to the heathen who have never heard the gospel, but to those who reject it.
He hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. 1 Tim. v.
scriptures: And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
Tit 1:16
They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.
Rom 1:28
And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 5:8 measures a man's creed by his provision for his own house, and that measurement is quietly dropped wherever unbelief is treated as a merely intellectual position.
corruption_paragraphs: Unbelief is habitually presented as a conclusion honestly reached — a man weighed the evidence and was not persuaded — and on that account as morally neutral. Romans 1 refuses the account. Men did not like to retain God in their knowledge; the mind was given over because the will had already turned. Unbelief is therefore not the absence of a proof but the suppression of one, and Scripture treats it as culpable throughout. This matters pastorally because the neutral account produces a limp evangelism that argues a man into assent and never calls him to repent, when the New Testament everywhere commands both together: repent, and believe the gospel. The apostle's question in 2 Corinthians is likewise not a counsel about compatibility but a statement about foundations. Christ and Belial have no concord, and where there is no concord there can be no yoke.

The sharper corruption is the one 1 Timothy 5:8 was written against, and it runs in the professing church rather than outside it. A man may hold every article of the confession, attend faithfully, speak well of the doctrines of grace, and leave his own household unprovided for — and Paul's verdict is that he has denied the faith and stands worse than an unbeliever. The verse cuts two ways in our own moment. It rebukes the man who spends himself on ministry or on reputation while his wife and children go without his labour, and it rebukes the notion that a family's support is a matter of preference or of arrangement rather than a duty laid on the head of the house. The word provide is wide: bread, protection, instruction, and the ordering of a household under God. Where the doctrine is confessed and the door of one's own house is neglected, the doctrine has been denied in the only language the neighbours can read.
roots_summary: Greek apistos (G571), unbelieving, faithless, rendered infidel in both Authorized Version occurrences; from a-, not, and pistis (G4102), faith.
roots_lines: Greek apistos (G571) — without faith, unbelieving; rendered infidel at 2 Corinthians 6:15 and 1 Timothy 5:8, and unbeliever elsewhere.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, the thing the infidel lacks and the professor of 1 Timothy 5:8 is said to have denied.
Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown; used of the man who does not provide for his own; 1 Timothy 5:8, 2 Timothy 2:12.
Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be unequally yoked, the figure of two beasts of different kinds under one bar; 2 Corinthians 6:14.
Greek Belial (G955) — worthlessness, a name for the evil one set opposite Christ in the same verse; 2 Corinthians 6:15.
usage: “What part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” — no shared foundation, therefore no yoke.
“Worse than an infidel” — the professor who leaves his own house unprovided.
“In works they deny him” — the confession the neighbours can actually read.

pos: n. pl. (those who set at nought; in Acts, despisers of the work of God; in Timothy, despisers of those that are good)
etymology: From Latin despicere, to look down upon, through Old French despire. The Greek at Acts 13:41 is kataphronetes, one who thinks down on a thing; at 2 Timothy 3:3 aphilagathos, not a lover of good.
biblical_def: Paul closes his sermon at Antioch with a warning out of Habakkuk: “Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you” (Act 13:41). The despiser is not the man who has never heard. He is the man in the synagogue who has heard the work of God declared and thinks down on it — and the sentence is that he shall wonder, and perish, and still not believe, though the thing be told him plainly. Timothy's list gives the other face of the word: among the marks of the last days are men “Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). The two despisings belong together. A man who thinks down on God's work will very soon think down on God's people, because goodness in another is a standing rebuke to a heart that has already dismissed the standard. Paul asks the Romans the question that exposes the root: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” (Rom 2:4). Mercy delayed is read as mercy not meant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to despise as to contemn, to scorn, to disdain, to have the lowest opinion of; a despiser is therefore one who contemns or scorns.
webster_full: DESPISE, v.t. [L. despicio; de and specio, to look.] To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.
Fools despise wisdom and instruction. Prov. i.
DESPISER, n. One who despises; a contemner; a scorner.
Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish. Acts xiii.
scriptures: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
Rom 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
He that despised Moses' law died without mercy under two or three witnesses:
corruption_summary: Despising is treated as a matter of taste rather than of judgment, though Acts 13:41 sets it directly under a sentence of perishing.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears despise as an emotion — a strong dislike, a matter of temperament — and so hears Paul's warning as intemperate. Scripture uses the word for a settled act of the judgment: to weigh a thing and rate it beneath notice. That is why it can be commanded against and punished. Esau despised his birthright, and the text does not describe a feeling but a transaction; he sold what he had rated low. Contempt for the work of God is the same transaction repeated with a greater object, and Habakkuk's sentence, which Paul reapplies at Antioch, is that such a man will watch the work go forward, marvel at it, and still not believe it. The judgment on despising is very often to be left with the despised thing still unbelieved.

Second Timothy names a species of the sin that respectable men still permit themselves: to be despisers of those that are good. The Greek is literally not-lovers-of-good, and it sits in a list beside fierceness and false accusing, which is where it belongs, for contempt for the godly is the last defence of a conscience that will not repent. It shows itself as the ready sneer at the strict, the practised amusement at the man who keeps his word at cost to himself, the assumption that visible seriousness about holiness must be hypocrisy or ambition. Romans 2:4 exposes the root and offers the remedy in the same breath. What is despised there is the riches of God's goodness, forbearance and longsuffering — a man reads God's patience as indifference and concludes there is nothing to answer for. The apostle answers that the goodness of God leads to repentance, and that a mercy misread as permission is being spent, not escaped.
roots_summary: Greek kataphronetes (G2707), a despiser, one who thinks down on a thing; aphilagathos (G865), not a lover of good; Hebrew bazah (H959), to hold in contempt.
roots_lines: Greek kataphronetes (G2707) — a despiser, from kata, down, and phroneo, to think; Acts 13:41, quoting Habakkuk 1:5.
Greek aphilagathos (G865) — not a lover of good, rendered despisers of those that are good; 2 Timothy 3:3.
Greek kataphroneo (G2706) — to think down on, to despise; used of despising the riches of God's goodness and of despising one master for another; Romans 2:4, Matthew 6:24.
Hebrew bazah (H959) — to hold in contempt, to disesteem; Esau despised his birthright, and the LORD's name is despised by careless priests; Genesis 25:34, Malachi 1:6.
Hebrew naats (H5006) — to spurn, to provoke by contempt; the sin of David's house that gave the enemies of the LORD occasion to blaspheme; 2 Samuel 12:14.
usage: “Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish” — contempt for the work of God under sentence.
“Despisers of those that are good” — the sneer at the godly as a mark of the last days.
“Despisest thou the riches of his goodness” — patience misread as permission.

pos: n. pl. (vaunters; men who make an empty show of what they are or have)
etymology: From Middle English bosten, to brag. The Greek alazon named the wandering quack who claimed cures he could not perform — a pretender whose word outruns his substance.
biblical_def: Boasters appear in both of the great catalogues of a society under judgment. Romans lists them among the marks of men given over: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents” (Rom 1:30). Second Timothy places them at the head of the perilous times: “For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2). In both lists the boaster stands next to the proud, and the order is instructive: pride is the root in the heart, boasting is the fruit in the mouth. James names the sin and passes sentence in a sentence: “But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil” (Jas 4:16). He is not condemning cheerfulness but the particular gladness a man takes in his own arrangements for tomorrow, as though the breath in his lungs were his own possession. The Psalmist sees the same tongue and asks God to deal with it: “The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things” (Psa 12:3). Scripture leaves one boast standing — the man who glories in the LORD — and destroys every other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a boaster as one who boasts, glories, or vaunts ostentatiously; to boast is to vaunt, to brag, to display one's own worth or actions in high terms.
webster_full: BOAST, v.i. To brag, or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display, in speech, of one's own worth, property, or actions.
2. To glory; to speak with laudable pride and exultation of meritorious persons or things.
BOASTER, n. One who boasts, glories or vaunts ostentatiously.
Covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers. 2 Tim. iii.
scriptures: Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Jas 4:16
But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.
Psa 12:3
The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things:
corruption_summary: Boasting has been rehabilitated as confidence and self-advertisement made a duty of the working life, while James calls the rejoicing itself evil.
corruption_paragraphs: The alazon of the Greek was a figure of contempt: the travelling pretender whose claims could not be cashed. Our own age has made his manner a discipline. A man is taught to present himself, to build a name, to speak of his work in terms that outrun it, and to call the whole performance confidence; the boaster is no longer the man everyone laughs at but the man everyone is advised to imitate. Scripture does not answer this with false modesty, which is only pride wearing a plainer coat. It answers with a question that removes the ground of boasting altogether: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? If a man's gift, health, wit and opportunity were all given, then boasting is not an overstatement of his merit but a misattribution of God's. That is why Paul can allow one glorying and no other, and why the boasts of Romans 1 stand in a list of men who did not like to retain God in their knowledge.

James is dealing with a boast so ordinary that it hardly sounds like one: to day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain. There is no bragging in it, only planning — and the apostle calls the rejoicing evil. What offends is not the plan but the assumed possession of the time in which to execute it, when the man does not know what shall be on the morrow and his life is a vapour. The correction he gives is not to stop planning but to plan under God: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. That little clause, said honestly, is the death of boasting in a Christian's speech, because it acknowledges every hour as a loan. The corruption to name here is the reverse habit, common in professing circles, of announcing what God is going to do through a man as though the announcement secured it. Boasting about the future in religious language is still boasting about the future.
roots_summary: Greek alazon (G213), a vaunting pretender; alazoneia (G212), the boasting itself; set against kauchaomai (G2744) rightly directed — glorying in the LORD.
roots_lines: Greek alazon (G213) — a boaster, a braggart whose claim exceeds his substance; Romans 1:30, 2 Timothy 3:2.
Greek alazoneia (G212) — boasting, vainglory; the pride of life that is not of the Father; James 4:16, 1 John 2:16.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to glory, to boast; forbidden of self and commanded of the Lord; 1 Corinthians 1:31, Galatians 6:14.
Greek huperephanos (G5244) — proud, showing oneself above others; the companion word in both catalogues; Romans 1:30, James 4:6.
Hebrew halal (H1984) — to shine, to praise, and in the reflexive to boast; let not the wise man glory in his wisdom; Jeremiah 9:23-24.
usage: “Covetous, boasters, proud” — the mouth's fruit standing next to the heart's root.
“All such rejoicing is evil” — the ordinary boast of a year's plans.
“The tongue that speaketh proud things” — what the LORD will cut off.

pos: n. pl. (those who turn away after having belonged; apostates within the covenant people)
etymology: French revolter, from Latin revolvere, to roll back. The Hebrew sarar and sur carry the same picture: to turn aside, to be stubborn, to go back from a place one had come to.
biblical_def: A revolter is not an outsider. The word belongs to the covenant people and names those who turned. Jeremiah's indictment is total: “They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters” (Jer 6:28). The metals are the point — the assayer looked for silver and found base metal all through. Hosea sees the same men at their worst, and with a terrible competence: “And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all” (Hos 5:2). Profound is the word for depth and skill; a people who once knew the law can apply real intelligence to evil. Later Hosea puts the revolt at the very top of the nation: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more: all their princes are revolters” (Hos 9:15). Isaiah opens his prophecy with the same grief in family terms: “I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me” (Isa 1:2). The tragedy of revolt is measured by the privilege it turns from.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revolter as one who changes sides; one who abandons a party or a cause to which he had adhered, or who renounces his allegiance.
webster_full: REVOLT, v.i. To fall off or turn from one to another.
2. To renounce allegiance and subjection to one's prince or state; to reject the authority of a sovereign.
REVOLTER, n. One who changes sides; one who abandons a party or a cause; an apostate.
They are all grievous revolters. Jer. vi.
scriptures: Jer 6:28
They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters.
Hos 5:2
And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all.
Hos 9:15
All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more: all their princes are revolters.
Isa 1:2
Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.
corruption_summary: Turning from the faith one was raised in is now narrated as growth and honesty, though Scripture calls it revolt and grieves over it as a father grieves.
corruption_paragraphs: The public account of leaving the faith has been rewritten in our lifetime. What Jeremiah calls revolt is now told as a story of a man coming into his own — he examined what he had been given, found it wanting, and had the courage to walk. The telling is careful never to name a doctrine that was disproved, because usually none was; what changed was allegiance. Scripture is not impressed by the narrative and it is not fooled by the vocabulary. Hosea's revolters are profound, which is to say clever, articulate, capable of an impressive case; the prophet does not deny their ability, he denies their innocence. And Jeremiah's image of the assay is the answer to every claim that the departure simply revealed what was always there: the fire found brass and iron because brass and iron were what the ore contained. First John says the same thing without heat — they went out from us because they were not of us.

The second thing to name is where Hosea locates the revolt: all their princes are revolters. The rot did not begin with the common people; it came down from the men in office. That is the ordinary pattern in the histories, and it is a warning to every eldership. A congregation is rarely more faithful than its teachers for long. Against this the Lord sets the promise that makes recovery possible and that no revolter has ever exhausted: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely. The doctrine of perseverance is not the claim that no professing man ever walks away — the prophets and the apostles say plainly that many do — but that no one whom the Father gave to the Son is finally lost. The right use of the word revolter is therefore self-examination before it is a label for someone else.
roots_summary: Hebrew sarar (H5637), to be stubborn, to turn away; sur (H5493), to turn aside; meshubah (H4878), backsliding, the noun of the same turning.
roots_lines: Hebrew sarar (H5637) — to turn away, to be stubborn or rebellious; the stubborn and rebellious son, and the revolting people; Deuteronomy 21:18, Jeremiah 6:28.
Hebrew sur (H5493) — to turn aside, to depart; used of princes who are revolters and companions of thieves; Hosea 9:15, Isaiah 1:23.
Hebrew meshubah (H4878) — backsliding, turning back; the word of the promise that God will heal it; Jeremiah 3:22, Hosea 14:4.
Hebrew marad (H4775) — to rebel, to revolt against a sovereign; the rebellion of Zedekiah against Babylon and of Israel against God; Ezekiel 17:15.
Greek apostasia (G646) — a standing away, apostasy; the falling away that precedes the day of Christ; 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
usage: “They are all grievous revolters” — the assay that found brass and iron.
“The revolters are profound to make slaughter” — ability without allegiance.
“All their princes are revolters” — the rot that came down from the men in office.

pos: adj. (given to excess in eating; the charge falsely laid against the Son of man)
etymology: Latin gluttire, to swallow or gulp down. The Greek phagos is simply an eater, used as an insult: a man defined by his appetite.
biblical_def: The word enters the New Testament as a slander against Christ. “The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children” (Mat 11:19); Luke records it in the same terms (Luk 7:34). The context is the Lord's complaint that His generation could not be pleased: John came neither eating nor drinking and they said he had a devil; the Son of man came eating and drinking and they called Him a glutton. The charge tells us nothing about Christ and everything about men who had already decided. Yet the sin itself is real and Scripture is severe about it. “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). Under the law a son past correction was charged in these very words before the elders: “This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard” (Deu 21:20). The Bible is not squeamish about eating — it gives feasts, and it gives a Supper — but it knows the difference between a table received with thanksgiving and a belly made a god.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gluttonous as given to excessive eating; greedy of eating; insatiable; and a glutton as one who indulges to excess in eating.
webster_full: GLUTTON, n. [L. gluto, from glutio, to swallow.] One who indulges to excess in eating.
2. One eager of anything to excess.
GLUTTONOUS, a. Given to excessive eating; greedy of eating; insatiable.
Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber. Matt. xi.
scriptures: The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.
Luk 7:34
The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners!
For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
And they shall say unto the elders of his city, This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard.
corruption_summary: The one sin of appetite the modern church will not name is the one the law named first, while the charge Christ actually bore — friend of publicans and sinners — is worn as a license.
corruption_paragraphs: Gluttony has quietly left the pulpit's list. Drunkenness is still preached against; excess at the table is treated as a matter of health, taste, or metabolism, and any mention of it is felt to be unkind. Two errors meet here and both must be refused. The first is the silence itself, which leaves a real work of the flesh unnamed — Paul writes of men whose god is their belly, and Proverbs joins the glutton to the drunkard in one sentence of consequence. The second error is the opposite overcorrection, in which weight becomes the measure of holiness and the thin man is assumed to be temperate. Scripture's category is not the shape of the body but the rule of the appetite: whether a man eats to the glory of God with thanksgiving, or is governed by what he wants. Fasting has all but disappeared from ordinary practice, and its disappearance is the plainest evidence that the appetite is not being examined at all.

The other corruption runs from the slander itself. Because our Lord was called a glutton and a winebibber for eating with publicans and sinners, some argue that any charge of excess against a Christian is proof of the accuser's pharisaism, and that being disreputable is itself a mark of gospel faithfulness. The text will not carry it. Christ ate with sinners and never sinned at their tables; He was falsely accused, which is a different thing from being rightly accused and dismissing it. His own answer is the standard: wisdom is justified of her children — the vindication comes from what the life produces, not from the accusation being loud. A man whose conduct is genuinely temperate may be slandered and should bear it. A man whose appetite genuinely rules him may not hide behind the slander that was laid on his Master.
roots_summary: Greek phagos (G5314), an eater, a glutton; Hebrew zalal (H2151), to be loose or worthless, used of the glutton; both set against egkrateia (G1466), temperance.
roots_lines: Greek phagos (G5314) — a glutton, literally an eater; used only in the slander against Christ; Matthew 11:19, Luke 7:34.
Hebrew zalal (H2151) — to shake out, to be loose, hence to squander or be a glutton; Deuteronomy 21:20, Proverbs 23:21.
Greek koilia (G2836) — the belly; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame; Philippians 3:19.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — temperance, self-mastery; the fruit of the Spirit that governs appetite; Galatians 5:23.
Greek oinopotes (G3630) — a winebibber, the companion charge in the same slander; Matthew 11:19.
usage: “Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber” — the slander a generation laid on Christ.
“The drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty” — appetite and its wages.
“Wisdom is justified of her children” — the vindication that comes from fruit, not from volume.

pos: adj. (ungrateful; not returning thanks for benefits received)
etymology: English un-, not, with thankful, from thank, akin to think — gratitude is a work of the mind before it is a word of the mouth. The Greek acharistos is the negative of charis, grace: the man who does not acknowledge a favour.
biblical_def: Ingratitude is not a small fault in Scripture; it stands at the head of the descent in Romans and in the middle of the marks of the last days. “For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2). Romans traces the whole ruin of the heathen mind back to this point: “Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom 1:21). The darkening of the mind followed the failure of thanks. Most striking of all is where the Lord Jesus places the word: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil” (Luk 6:35). God's own kindness reaches the ungrateful, and that is offered as the pattern for a Christian's dealings with men who will never say thank you. Against all of it stands the plain command: “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you” (1Th 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unthankful as ungrateful; not thankful; not making acknowledgments for good received; and unthankfulness as neglect or omission of acknowledgment for favors.
webster_full: UNTHANKFUL, a. Ungrateful; not thankful; not making acknowledgments for good received.
He is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Luke vi.
UNTHANKFULLY, adv. Without thanks; ungratefully.
UNTHANKFULNESS, n. Neglect or omission of acknowledgment for good received; ingratitude.
scriptures: For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Luk 6:35

But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
corruption_summary: Gratitude has been reduced to a private discipline that improves the one who practises it, when Romans 1:21 presents thanklessness as the hinge on which a mind turns dark.
corruption_paragraphs: Thankfulness is now widely recommended, and recommended for the wrong reason. It is taught as a practice that benefits the practitioner — keep a list of good things, notice them, and your outlook improves. Everything in that account is true except what matters: it has no object. Thanks in Scripture is always thanks to someone, and its absence is not a mood but a refusal to name a Giver. That is exactly Paul's argument. Men knew God, glorified Him not as God, neither were thankful, and from that point the reasoning went vain and the heart went dark. Ingratitude is therefore not the last symptom of unbelief but one of its first causes, and a discipline of noticing blessings while declining to name the One who sent them is not obedience to 1 Thessalonians 5:18 but a more comfortable way of doing the thing Romans 1 describes.

The second corruption is inside the church, and it is the assumption that thanks is owed only when the providence is pleasant. The apostle writes in every thing, which is not the same as for every thing; a Christian is not commanded to call evil good, but he is commanded to give thanks in the middle of it, because the God who governs the loss is the same God who gave the mercies. Where that is lost the household becomes a place of complaint, and complaint is contagious in a way gratitude has to be taught. The Lord's own example in Luke 6:35 sets the standard higher still: God is kind unto the unthankful. A man who will only be generous to those who acknowledge it has not yet learned how he was treated himself, for the whole of his salvation was given to him while he was still ungrateful.
roots_summary: Greek acharistos (G884), unthankful, from a-, not, and charis, grace or favour; set against eucharisteo (G2168), to give thanks.
roots_lines: Greek acharistos (G884) — ungrateful, unthankful; used twice, of the last days and of those to whom God is nonetheless kind; 2 Timothy 3:2, Luke 6:35.
Greek eucharisteo (G2168) — to give thanks, to be grateful; the verb over the bread at the Supper; Luke 22:19, 1 Thessalonians 5:18.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, favour; the root the unthankful man denies by not acknowledging it.
Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to give thanks, literally to cast out the hand; the standing word of the Psalter's praise; Psalm 107:1.
Hebrew todah (H8426) — thanksgiving, a thank offering; sacrifice and gratitude joined in one word; Psalm 50:14.
usage: “Neither were thankful” — the hinge on which Romans 1 turns toward darkness.
“He is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil” — the pattern for dealing with men who never say thank you.
“In every thing give thanks” — in every thing, which is not the same as for every thing.

pos: n. pl. (covenant-breakers; men who will not be bound by an agreement they have made)
etymology: English truce, from Middle English trewes, pledges of faith, with breaker. The Greek aspondos means literally without a drink-offering — without the libation that sealed a treaty, and so a man with whom no terms can be made.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in the catalogue of the perilous times: “Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). Its neighbours in the list show the register. These are not petty offences but the dissolution of the bonds that hold a society upright: affection that no longer holds within a family, agreements that no longer hold between men, appetite that no longer holds within a man. Paul has already said what kind of season this is: “This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come” (2Ti 3:1). Romans uses the near-identical charge of the heathen mind: “Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31). Against this Scripture sets the man God receives, described by an oath he keeps at his own cost: “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4). Joshua's princes are the great narrative example. Deceived into a league with the Gibeonites, they still said, “We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them” (Jos 9:19) — and four hundred years later God avenged Saul's breach of that same word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a trucebreaker as one who violates a truce, covenant or engagement; a truce being a suspension of arms by agreement, and, more broadly, a pledge of faith between parties.
webster_full: TRUCE, n. [from trew, trewes, faith, pledge of faith.] A suspension of arms by agreement of the commanders; a temporary cessation of hostilities.
2. Intermission of action, pain or contest; temporary cessation.
TRUCEBREAKER, n. One who violates a truce, covenant or engagement.
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers. 2 Tim. iii.
scriptures: Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Jos 9:19
But all the princes said unto all the congregation, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them.
corruption_summary: An oath is now held to bind only while it still suits the one who swore it, which is precisely the definition of a trucebreaker.
corruption_paragraphs: The plainest place this shows is the marriage covenant, where vows are made in the language of permanence and dissolved on the ground that the parties have changed. The reasoning is always the same and it is always the reasoning of 2 Timothy 3:3: the agreement was made by a man who no longer exists, therefore it no longer binds. Scripture's answer is Psalm 15:4, which describes the citizen of God's hill by exactly the case that tests him — he swore, the swearing turned out to cost him, and he did not change. The verse assumes the hurt. An oath that costs nothing has not yet been kept. The same collapse works its way through commercial dealing, church membership, and the ordinary promises of a household, and in each case the word given is treated as a forecast of intention rather than a bond upon the will.

The Greek word carries a detail worth keeping. Aspondos is without a libation — treaties in the ancient world were sealed with a poured drink offering, so a man called aspondos is one with whom no terms can be struck at all: not merely a man who breaks a truce, but a man no truce can hold. That is the terminal stage, and it is why the word sits beside implacable in Romans 1:31. The remedy is not sterner contracts. It is a nature that keeps faith because it has been dealt with faithfully — and here the doctrine of the covenant is the whole comfort of the Christian, because the covenant of grace does not rest on the sinner's constancy but on the oath of God, who sware by himself since he could swear by no greater. A people who know they are held by an unbreakable word are the only people likely to keep their own.
roots_summary: Greek aspondos (G786), without a libation, admitting no truce; asunthetos (G802), covenant-breaking; Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear an oath.
roots_lines: Greek aspondos (G786) — without a drink offering, hence admitting of no truce or agreement; rendered trucebreakers; 2 Timothy 3:3.
Greek asunthetos (G802) — not put together, covenant-breaking; the parallel charge in the heathen catalogue; Romans 1:31.
Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear, to bind oneself by seven, that is by an oath; Joshua 9:19, Psalm 15:4.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant, a bond cut and sealed; the whole framework the trucebreaker despises; Genesis 15:18.
Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; God interposed himself by an oath to show the immutability of his counsel; Hebrews 6:17.
usage: “Trucebreakers, false accusers” — the bonds of a society coming apart in one list.
“He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” — the oath that costs, kept.
“We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel” — a word kept though it was got by deceit.

pos: adj. (not to be appeased; refusing to be reconciled)
etymology: Latin implacabilis, from in-, not, and placare, to appease or pacify. The man who cannot be brought to peace, however the offence is confessed or the amends offered.
biblical_def: The word appears once, at the bottom of Romans 1: “Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31). Every term in that line is a negative — the passage is describing not the presence of vice so much as the absence of the things that make men human, and implacability is the refusal of the peace that reconciliation offers. The next verse shows how deep it goes: such men know the judgment of God and “have pleasure in them that do them” (Rom 1:32). Set against this the Lord's parable, where the forgiven servant takes his fellow by the throat and hears the question that answers implacability for ever: “Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” (Mat 18:33). The wisdom from above is described in the exact opposite terms: “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits” (Jas 3:17). Easy to be intreated is the direct antonym of implacable; a Christian is to be a man whom an offending brother can approach. And the command is plainer still: “And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you” (Eph 4:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines implacable as not to be appeased or pacified; inexorable; stubborn or constant in enmity; and applied to passions, not to be subdued.
webster_full: IMPLACABLE, a. [L. implacabilis; in and placabilis, from placo, to appease.] Not to be appeased; that cannot be pacified and rendered peaceable; inexorable; stubborn or constant in enmity.
2. Not to be appeased or subdued; as implacable hatred; implacable enmity.
IMPLACABLENESS, n. The quality of not being appeasable; inexorableness; irreconcilable enmity.
Without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful. Rom. i.
scriptures: Rom 1:31
Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful:
Rom 1:32
Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them.
Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?
Eph 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
corruption_summary: Refusing reconciliation is now defended as the protection of oneself, and a settled unwillingness to be entreated is presented as a virtue rather than named as the sin of Romans 1:31.
corruption_paragraphs: A vocabulary has grown up in which permanent estrangement is described as a wise arrangement: the offender is cut off, the door is closed, and the closing is spoken of as strength. Some of what that vocabulary addresses is real, and Scripture provides for it — a man is not obliged to entrust himself again to one who has not repented, Paul names those from whom we are to turn away, and the church has the power to put a man out. But there is a difference between withholding trust from an unrepentant man and being a man who cannot be entreated at all, and Romans 1:31 names the second as one of the marks of a mind given over. The test is simple and searching: if the offender came, confessed the thing plainly, and sought peace, would he find a door? Where the honest answer is no, the position is not prudence, it is implacability, and it stands in a list with covenantbreaking and the loss of natural affection.

James gives the Christian standard in a phrase our language has almost lost: the wisdom from above is easy to be intreated. That does not mean gullible, and it does not mean soft on sin — the same verse puts first pure before then peaceable, and the order is not negotiable. It means approachable; a man to whom the person in the wrong can come. The reason the New Testament presses this so hard is not that offences are small but that the Christian's own case was hopeless. The servant in Matthew 18 was forgiven ten thousand talents and took his fellow by the throat for a hundred pence, and the Lord's question is the only argument the passage needs. A man who has truly reckoned what he was forgiven at the cross has lost the standing from which implacability can be maintained.
roots_summary: Greek aspondos (G786) in the Received Text at Romans 1:31, admitting no truce; contrasted with eupeithes (G2138), easy to be intreated, and eleemon (G1655), merciful.
roots_lines: Greek aspondos (G786) — without libation, admitting no terms of peace; rendered implacable at Romans 1:31 and trucebreakers at 2 Timothy 3:3.
Greek aneleemon (G415) — unmerciful, without pity; the companion word closing the same verse; Romans 1:31.
Greek eupeithes (G2138) — easily persuaded, easy to be intreated; the mark of the wisdom that is from above; James 3:17.
Greek katallasso (G2644) — to reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship; the work God did toward us in Christ; 2 Corinthians 5:18-19.
Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion in the inward parts; the pity the unforgiving servant had received and would not give; Matthew 18:27.
usage: “Without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” — the negatives that describe a mind given over.
“Easy to be intreated” — the direct antonym, and a mark of wisdom from above.
“Even as I had pity on thee” — the question that ends every argument for an unopenable door.
